disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is characterized by a continuous period of illness during which there is a major depressive episode concurrent with Criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking/behavior, and/or negative symptoms). There must be at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, distinguishing it from mood disorders with psychotic features, while mood episodes are present for the majority of the total duration of the illness, differentiating it from schizophrenia. The clinical course is typically chronic or relapsing, with variable functional impairment across work, relationships, and self-care, and onset can be linked to psychosocial stressors, health declines, or cumulative vulnerabilities. Depressive-type presentations often feature profound hopelessness and suicidality alongside the psychotic process, increasing risk for self-harm and delayed help-seeking.

narrative.personality: A curious, creatively minded tech veteran who values flexibility and quirky projects, but tends to be laid-back and intermittently disorganized in his routines.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Russell’s long-time contract with a local manufacturing firm was abruptly not renewed after a major ERP migration, leaving him feeling professionally discarded and increasingly anxious about his relevance in a rapidly changing tech landscape. At the same time, he found it harder to keep up with complex projects and multitasking demands, which he interpreted as evidence that his mind was "slipping," amplifying longstanding insecurities from an earlier divorce and a sense of aging out of the field he loved. As he withdrew from consulting opportunities, his days became unstructured, dominated by solitary tinkering with vintage machines and late-night online deep dives, during which his thinking grew more rigid and preoccupied, and his worldview gradually took on an increasingly dark, self-referential tone. Over the ensuing months, his creative pursuits lost their usual pleasure, his functioning eroded to the point of neglecting basic responsibilities, and he ultimately sought psychiatric care after frightening himself with how often he found himself planning ways not to wake up rather than face what he was convinced was a pointless, deteriorating future.
narrative.chief_complaint: I keep thinking about dying and different ways I could end my life, and it scares me how often that’s on my mind now.

narrative.personality: A structured, community-oriented retiree who takes quiet pride in his gardening, woodworking, and historical storytelling, and finds satisfaction in steady routines and helping others.
narrative.stressor: Approximately seventeen months ago, Victor lost a close friend from his church men’s group, a fellow widower who had been his daily walking partner and collaborator in oral-history projects, leaving a sudden void in his carefully organized routine. This loss stirred up older, unresolved grief over his divorce and earlier family deaths, and he began to question the point of preserving stories and traditions when so many of the people who cared about them were gone. Over time, he gradually pulled back from church committees, woodworking circles, and gardening club meetings, telling himself he was just "slowing down," yet noticing that days would pass without him touching his tools, tending his tomatoes, or calling the youth he once mentored. His family and pastor encouraged him to seek psychiatric care when they saw that his once-busy schedule had dwindled to long, idle days in front of the TV and unanswered invitations, and he admitted that the activities that used to give his life structure and meaning now felt strangely empty and uninviting.
narrative.chief_complaint: I don’t enjoy my gardening, woodworking, or church activities anymore; I just don’t feel like doing any of it these days.

narrative.personality: A calm, resilient, and curious retail worker who enjoys cooking, gardening, and quiet crafts, though she can be somewhat relaxed and disorganized in managing her own goals.
narrative.stressor: Around a year and five months ago, Sha’s household became increasingly strained when her husband was laid off and her teenage child began having academic and behavioral difficulties, placing new financial and emotional pressure on her as the primary earner. She took on extra shifts at the store while trying to support her family, leaving little time for her usual grounding routines of cooking elaborate meals, reading, and gardening, and she started to feel chronically overwhelmed and second-guessed in her decisions at home and at work. Under this sustained strain, she found it harder to follow conversations at the register, keep track of tasks, and make even small choices about bills or scheduling, which frightened her and led her to worry that something was fundamentally wrong with her mind. As conflicts at home escalated and her performance at work slipped enough for a supervisor to comment, she finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after realizing that her thinking felt increasingly foggy and unreliable, to the point that simple decisions that once felt effortless now left her stuck and distressed.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I feel like my mind is foggy and I can’t think straight or make even simple decisions the way I used to.
